Main.sentence: Federal lands are lands in the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States)___ owned and managed by the ___E:federal government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States)___ .

Pursuant to the ___E:Property Clause U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Property_Clause)___ of the ___E:United States Constitution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Constitution)___ ( ___E:Article 4 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Article_Four_of_the_United_States_Constitution#Clause_2:_Property_Clause)___ , section 3, clause 2), ___E:Congress U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress)___ has the power to retain, buy, sell, and regulate federal lands.
These powers have been recognized in a long series of ___E:United States Supreme Court U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Supreme_Court)___ decisions.

In Article I, Section 8, Clause 17 the United States Constitution empowers the federal government with exclusive legislative authority like that exercised for ___E:Washington D.C. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_D.C.)___ over "Places purchased by the Consent of the Legislature of the State in which the same shall be, for the erection of Forts, Magazines, Arsenals, Dock-yards, and other needful Buildings."
The federal government manages about 640 million acres (2.6 million km 2 ) of land in the United States, which is about 28% of the total land area of 2.27 billion acres (9.2 million km 2 ).

The majority of federal lands (610.1 million acres (2.469 million km 2 ) or 95 percent area in 2015) are administered by the ___E:Bureau of Land Management U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureau_of_Land_Management)___ (BLM), ___E:United States Fish and Wildlife Service U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Fish_and_Wildlife_Service)___ (FWS), ___E:National Park Service U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service)___ (NPS), or ___E:United States Forest Service U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Forest_Service)___ (USFS).

BLM, FWS, and NPS are part of the ___E:United States Department of the Interior U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_the_Interior)___ , while the Forest Service is part of the ___E:United States Department of Agriculture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Agriculture)___ .

An additional 11.4 million acres (46 thousand km 2 ) of land (about 2% of all federal land) is managed by the ___E:United States Department of Defense U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense)___ (DOD).
The majority of federal lands are located in ___E:Alaska U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska)___ and the ___E:Western U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_United_States)___ states.

The ___E:United States Supreme Court U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States)___ has upheld the broad powers of the federal government to deal with federal lands, for example having unanimously held in Kleppe v. New Mexico  that "the complete power that Congress has over federal lands under this clause necessarily includes the power to regulate and protect wildlife living there, state law notwithstanding."

Lands held by the United States ___E:in trust U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_trust)___ for ___E:Native American U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States)___ tribes are generally not considered public lands.

There are some 55 million acres (0.22 million km 2 ) of land held in trust by the federal government for Indian tribes and almost 11 million acres (45 thousand km 2 ) of land held in trust by the federal government for individual Natives.
Although the United States holds legal title to these lands, the tribe or individual holds beneficial title (the right to use and benefit from the property).

As a result, ___E:Indian Country U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Country)___ is "quasi-private, not public, land."  Nevertheless, "because the United States is a legal title holder, the federal government is a necessary part in all leases and dispositions of resources including trust land. For example, the secretary of the interior must approve any contract for payment or grant by an Indian tribe for services for the tribe 'relative to their lands' (25 U.S.C. § 81)."

The ___E:Land Ordinance of 1785 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_Ordinance_of_1785)___ and the ___E:Northwest Ordinance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Ordinance)___ of 1787 provided for the survey and settlement of the lands that the original ___E:Thirteen Colonies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteen_Colonies)___ ceded to the federal government after the ___E:American Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_War_of_Independence)___ .

As additional lands were acquired by the United States from ___E:Spain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain)___ , ___E:France U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France)___ , Native American Nations and other countries, the ___E:United States Congress U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress)___ directed that they be explored, surveyed, and made available for settlement.
During the Revolutionary War, military bounty land was promised to soldiers who fought for the colonies.

After the war, the ___E:Treaty of Paris of 1783 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Paris_(1783))___ , signed by the United States, the ___E:Kingdom of Great Britain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Great_Britain)___ , ___E:France U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France)___ , and ___E:Spain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain)___ , ceded territory to the United States.
In the 1780s, other states relinquished their own claims to land in modern-day ___E:Ohio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio)___ .
By this time, the United States needed revenue to function.
Land was sold so that the government would have money to survive.
In order to sell the land, surveys needed to be conducted.
The ___E:Land Ordinance of 1785 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_Ordinance_of_1785)___ instructed a geographer to oversee this work as undertaken by a group of surveyors.
The first years of surveying were completed by trial and error; once the territory of Ohio had been surveyed, a modern public land survey system had been developed.

In 1812, Congress established the ___E:United States General Land Office U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_General_Land_Office)___ as part of the ___E:Department of the Treasury U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_the_Treasury)___ to oversee the disposition of these federal lands.
By the early 1800s, promised bounty land claims were finally fulfilled.

In the 19th century, other bounty land and homestead laws were enacted to dispose of federal land.   These included, among others, the ___E:Homestead Act of 1862 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homestead_Act_of_1862)___ and the Desert Lands Entry Act of 1877.  Several different types of patents existed.

These include cash entry, credit, homestead, Indian, military warrants, mineral certificates, private land claims, railroads, state selections, swamps, town sites, and town lots.  A system of local land offices spread throughout the territories, patenting land that was surveyed via the corresponding ___E:Office of the Surveyor General U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surveyor_General_of_the_Northwest_Territory)___ of a particular territory.
This pattern gradually spread across the entire United States.

Homestead entries peaked in 1910, when they amounted to 18.3 million acres (0.074 million km 2 ), and sharply declined after 1935 and were eliminated in 1986.  The laws that spurred mass federal land transfers, with the exception of the ___E:General Mining Law of 1872 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Mining_Law_of_1872)___ and the ___E:Desert Land Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desert_Land_Act)___ of 1877, have since been repealed or superseded.

Between 1781 and 2018, the federal government divested itself of estimated 1.29 billion acres (5.2 million km 2 ) of public domain land.  The vast majority (97%) of transfers of federal land to private ownership occurred before 1940.  Beginning in the early 20th century, U.S. government policy shifted from disposing of public land to retaining and managing it.  Congress took additional steps toward recognizing the value of the assets on public lands and directed the ___E:Executive Branch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Branch)___ to manage activities on the remaining public lands.

The ___E:Mineral Leasing Act of 1920 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mineral_Leasing_Act_of_1920)___ allowed leasing, exploration, and production of selected commodities, such as ___E:coal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal)___ , ___E:oil U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum)___ , ___E:gas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas)___ , and ___E:sodium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium)___ to take place on public lands.

The ___E:Taylor Grazing Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Grazing_Act)___ of 1934 established the ___E:United States Grazing Service U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Grazing_Service)___ to ___E:manage the public rangelands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rangeland_management)___ by establishment of advisory boards that set grazing fees.   The ___E:Oregon and California Revested Lands Sustained Yield Management Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_and_California_Railroad_Revested_Lands)___ of 1937, commonly referred as the O&C Act, required sustained ___E:yield management U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yield_management)___ of the timberlands in western Oregon.

The ___E:Sagebrush Rebellion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagebrush_Rebellion)___ movement in the ___E:Western United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_United_States)___ in the 1970s and the 1980s sought major changes to federal land control, use, and disposal policy in 13 western states in which federal land holdings include between 20% and 85% of a state's area.   Supporters of the movement wanted more state and local control over the lands, if not outright transfer of them to state and local authorities and/or privatization.
From 1990 to 2018, the overall acreage held by the federal government decreased by 4.9% (i.e., from 646.9 million acres (2.618 million km 2 ) to 615.3 million acres (2.490 million km 2 )).

Over that time period, the federal acreage held by the Bureau of Land Management and Department of Defense decreased by 10.2% and 56.8%, respectively, and the federal acreage held by the Forest Service, Fish and Wildlife Service, and National Park Service increased by 0.8%, 2.7%, and 5.0%, respectively.

Over the 1990–2018 time period, the largest decline in federal acreage was in Alaska (a decrease of 9.4%, or 23.0 million acres (0.093 million km 2 )) and in the 11 contiguous states of the West (a 3% decrease in federal land, or 10.7 million acres (0.043 million km 2 )).
The four primary federal land holders are:

The fifth largest federal landowner is the ___E:United States Department of Defense U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense)___ , which owns, leases, or possessed 26.1 million acres (0.106 million km 2 ) worldwide, of which 8.8 million acres (0.036 million km 2 ) are located in the United States (this figure excluded ___E:United States Army Corps of Engineers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Corps_of_Engineers)___ land).
DoD thus administers approximately 1% of federal land. DOD land is mostly ___E:military bases U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_bases)___ and reservations.

The largest single DOD-owned, all-land tract is the 2.3-million-acre ___E:White Sands Missile Range U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Sands_Missile_Range)___ in ___E:New Mexico U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico)___ .

Together, the BLM, FWS, NPS, Forest Service, and DOD manage about 96% of federal land.  The remaining 4% of federal land is controlled by other federal agencies, including the United States Army Corps of Engineers, the ___E:Bureau of Reclamation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureau_of_Reclamation)___ , the ___E:United States Postal Service U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service)___ , the ___E:National Aeronautics and Space Administration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Aeronautics_and_Space_Administration)___ , and the ___E:U.S. Department of Energy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Department_of_Energy)___ .
Federal land is concentrated in the ___E:Western United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_United_States)___ .

Nationwide, the federal government owns 27.4% of all land area. There are significant variations regionally; the federal government owns 61.3% of the land area in Alaska, 46.4% of the land area in the 11 ___E:contiguous U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_contiguity)___ Western states; and 4.2% of the land area of other states.

The state with the highest percentage of land held by the federal government is ___E:Nevada U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevada)___ (80.1%); the states with the lowest percentage of land held by the federal government are ___E:Connecticut U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut)___ and ___E:Iowa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa)___ (0.3%).

In the United States, acquired lands refer to a category of ___E:public lands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_lands)___ under federal management that were obtained by the ___E:federal government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States)___ through purchase, ___E:condemnation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eminent_domain)___ , gift, or exchange.
In the United States, federal lands are often used for ___E:environmental conservation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_Conservation)___ .
The administration of Joe Biden turned into ___E:protected areas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protected_area)___ 12.5 million acres in 2023 alone.
